definitions.definition: Einstein's theory that gravity is caused by the bending of space and time around massive objects.
definitions.example: Like a heavy ball on a trampoline making the surface curve, Earth curves space around it, pulling the Moon into orbit.
definitions.first_appearance: Einstein's General Relativity

definitions.definition: An invisible field that gives particles their mass by interacting with them.
definitions.example: Like moving through honey: the more a particle interacts with the field, the heavier it becomes.
definitions.first_appearance: The Higgs Field

definitions.definition: The world's largest and most powerful particle accelerator, a 17-mile ring under France and Switzerland that smashes particles together at near light speed.

definitions.first_appearance: The Higgs Field

definitions.definition: A set of equations and rules used to describe how something works.
definitions.example: Like the rules of chess that define how each piece moves, a mathematical framework defines how a physical system behaves.

definitions.definition: A proposed field of study that combines physics and theology, claiming that the same mathematical laws govern both the physical and spiritual worlds.

definitions.definition: A measure of how aligned or unified something is with truth and reality.

definitions.definition: Unearned help or restoration that comes from outside a person, not from their own effort.

definitions.definition: A measure of disorder or randomness in a system; things naturally tend to become more disordered over time.

definitions.definition: The immaterial, self-aware part of a person that is the center of their identity and consciousness.

definitions.definition: The entire span of time from beginning to end.

definitions.definition: Active trust and participation that turns possibility into reality.

definitions.definition: An equation where variables are multiplied together, so if any one variable is zero, the whole result is zero.
definitions.example: Like a chain: if any link breaks, the whole chain fails.

definitions.definition: A mapping between two systems that preserves all structural relationships, meaning they are the same in form even if they look different on the surface.
definitions.example: Like a song played in two different keys: the notes change, but the melody and structure are identical.

definitions.definition: A way of pairing each element of one set with an element of another set.
definitions.example: Like matching each student in a class to their own desk.

definitions.definition: How a system behaves at its limits or edges.
definitions.example: Like what happens to a rubber band when you stretch it to its breaking point.
definitions.first_appearance: An isomorphism is a mapping between two systems

definitions.definition: Features of a system that remain unchanged when you transform it in some way, like rotating or reflecting it.
definitions.example: Like a snowflake that looks the same when you rotate it 60 degrees.
definitions.first_appearance: An isomorphism is a mapping between two systems

definitions.definition: The rules that determine what quantities stay constant in a system, like energy or momentum.
definitions.example: Like a bank account: money can move around, but the total amount stays the same unless deposits or withdrawals happen.
definitions.first_appearance: An isomorphism is a mapping between two systems

definitions.definition: Equations that describe how a quantity changes over time or space.
definitions.example: Like a recipe that tells you how the temperature of a cup of coffee changes every minute as it cools.
definitions.first_appearance: The Ten Laws of the framework

definitions.definition: The law that says disorder (entropy) in a closed system always increases over time.
definitions.example: Like your room getting messier on its own, never tidier, unless you put in effort.
definitions.first_appearance: Boltzmann derived the second law of thermodynamics in the 1870s

definitions.definition: The mathematical study of how information is measured, stored, and communicated.
definitions.example: Like figuring out the best way to compress a file or send a message without errors.
definitions.first_appearance: Shannon formalized information theory in 1948

definitions.definition: The underlying material or medium in which something exists or operates.
definitions.example: Like the paper a story is printed on versus the digital screen it's read on — different substrates, same story.

definitions.definition: A number equal to 1 followed by 18 zeros (1,000,000,000,000,000,000).
definitions.example: Like the number of grains of sand on all the beaches on Earth, roughly.
definitions.first_appearance: One in a hundred quintillion.

definitions.definition: A physical quantity that has a value at every point in space and time.
definitions.example: Like a magnetic field around a magnet: you can't see it, but it affects things near it.
definitions.first_appearance: When you propose a new field in physics

definitions.definition: Answers to equations that don't blow up to infinity or behave chaotically; they stay within reasonable bounds.

definitions.definition: Not growing without bound or exploding to infinity.

definitions.definition: A disagreement between two different measurements of how fast the universe is expanding.
definitions.example: Like two stopwatches timing the same race but giving different finishing times, and no one knows why.
definitions.first_appearance: There is a crisis in cosmology right now called the Hubble tension.

definitions.definition: A statistical measure of how confident a result is; 5 sigma means there's only a 1 in 3.5 million chance the result is a fluke.
definitions.example: Like flipping a coin and getting heads 20 times in a row — that's so unlikely it's probably not a coincidence.
definitions.first_appearance: Two precise measurements of the universe's expansion rate disagree by 5 sigma.

definitions.definition: The study of the origin, structure, and evolution of the universe as a whole.
definitions.example: Like studying the entire history of the universe from the Big Bang to now.

definitions.definition: A measure of how strongly gravity acts in a given situation.
definitions.example: Like the strength of a magnet's pull, but for gravity.

definitions.definition: The Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument, a telescope that maps millions of galaxies to study dark energy.
definitions.example: Like a giant camera that takes a 3D picture of the universe to see how it's expanding.

definitions.definition: A mysterious force that is causing the universe to expand faster and faster.
definitions.example: Like an invisible anti-gravity pushing everything apart.

definitions.definition: An experiment designed to prove a theory wrong if it is wrong.

definitions.first_appearance: with a live falsification test coming in October 2026

definitions.definition: When a small change in one variable causes a disproportionately large change in the result.
definitions.example: Like a tiny crack in a dam that suddenly causes the whole dam to burst.

definitions.definition: The idea that the whole system must be considered, not just individual parts.
definitions.example: Like a car: all parts must work together; a missing wheel means the car doesn't move at all.
definitions.first_appearance: The holistic requirement is mathematically enforced

definitions.definition: A mathematical law that defines the maximum rate at which information can be transmitted without error over a noisy channel.
definitions.example: Like the maximum number of words you can shout across a noisy room and still be understood.
definitions.first_appearance: Shannon's channel capacity theorem is one of the most proven results in the history of mathematics.

definitions.definition: People or things that pass information from one place to another.
definitions.example: Like a game of telephone where each person whispers to the next.

definitions.definition: How accurately something is copied or transmitted.
definitions.example: Like the quality of a photocopy: high fidelity means it looks just like the original.

definitions.definition: A theory that measures how complex a piece of information is by the length of the shortest computer program that can produce it.
definitions.example: Like a simple pattern like 'ABABAB' is less complex than a random string like 'A7g!Qp' because it can be described with fewer instructions.
definitions.first_appearance: This is Kolmogorov complexity theory applied to the truth-falsehood distinction.

definitions.definition: Negative entropy; something that reduces disorder or increases order in a system.
definitions.example: Like a refrigerator that keeps food from spoiling by removing heat and maintaining order.
definitions.first_appearance: Grace is a negentropy term.

definitions.definition: Systems that involve heat, work, and energy transfer.
definitions.example: Like a steam engine or a pot of boiling water.
definitions.first_appearance: The second law governs moral and informational systems the same way it governs thermodynamic systems.

definitions.definition: The principle that certain pairs of properties, like position and momentum, cannot both be known exactly at the same time.

definitions.definition: The limits on how precisely something can be known.

definitions.definition: Information collected by observing the natural world, not from theory or simulation.
definitions.example: Like recording the temperature every day for a year rather than guessing what it might be.
